sources.citation: Dutton, Tom. 1985. Police Motu: iena sivarai (its story). Port Moresby: University of Papua New Guinea Press. 297 pp. Ch. 2 sec. 2.2 'The HTL(E)', pp. 22-29.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on HTL(E) stress. The HTL(E) section (pp. 22-29) gives a comparative HTL(E)/Toaripi sentence table and the grammatical pidgin features; the only phonological remark (p. 28) is that HTL(E) 'varies much more in pronunciation than Toaripi or other Eleman languages and Motu do' (b~m, l~n~v alternations). The book's one stress statement (Ch. 1, p. ~14) concerns Motu proper (hahine/kekeni plural marked by first-syllable stress vs second-last-syllable stress in the singular), not the pidgin. Footnote 5 (p. 239) says the HTL(E) description rests on Dutton & Kakare 1977 and Dutton 1978, 1979,…

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom. 1982. Towards a history of the hiri: some beginning linguistic observations. In T. Dutton (ed.), The Hiri in history: further aspects of long distance Motu trade in Central Papua (Pacific Research Monograph 8), 65-98. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on HTL(E) stress; history of HTL(E)/HTL(K), vocabulary-source estimates (about 80% Eleman), consonant-system table Motu/Toaripi/Orokolo/Koriki (p. 73). Only 'stressed' occurrence is inside a quoted Toaripi>Orokolo sound rule (p. 88), about the lexifier.

sources.citation: Dutton, T.E. 1978. Tracing the pidgin origin of Hiri (or Police) Motu: issues and problems. In S.A. Wurm & Lois Carrington (eds), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: proceedings (Pacific Linguistics C-61), 1351-1375. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on HTL stress. Compares syntactic pidgin features of Police Motu, HTL (from Dutton & Kakare 1977) and Solomon Islands Pidgin; the only stress remark (p. 1356) is that non-Central Police Motu speakers do not maintain the Motu stress distinctions in hahine 'woman' and kekeni 'girl' (singular vs plural).
